Question two. What back-of-the-envelope numbers should you estimate? The ones that turn product scale into load: requests per second, or QPS, then storage and bandwidth. One trick does most of the work. A million requests a day is about twelve a second. So assume ten million new links a day: about a hundred and twenty writes a second. Reads matter more. Most consumer systems are read-heavy, a hundred to one or more, so assume a hundred redirects per link: a billion a day, about twelve thousand a second. Size for the peak, not the average. Peaks often run two to three times higher, so take three: about thirty-five thousand redirects a second. Storage: a few hundred bytes a link, say five hundred, is five gigabytes a day, about nine terabytes in five years. Bandwidth: say half a kilobyte per redirect, and that peak is about seventeen megabytes a second. Neither is hard. This system is decided by its read traffic, and by how much of it a cache can answer.

Then keep one picture in your head: what each level of memory and network costs. Main memory, a hundred nanoseconds. An SSD read, a thousand times that. A round trip inside the data center, five times more again. So count the network hops in a request before anything else.

And quote latency as a percentile, never a mean. In a simulated sample of forty thousand requests, the median takes twenty-four milliseconds and the mean thirty-one, but one request in a hundred takes two hundred and eighty-six or more: the ninety-ninth percentile. A page that makes a hundred calls, each with that one-in-a-hundred chance, hits at least one on sixty-three percent of loads.
